title: Standing in the Middle
note: This is standing even towards enemies, strangers and friends without slipping from righteousness. It follows the last chapter because remembering a kindness can tempt you to lean towards the one who did it.

couplets.plain: What is called fairness is good, if you can give each side its due.
couplets.pm: The one righteousness called impartiality is good, if you can keep to your rule with each of the three groups, enemies, strangers and friends. “If you can” shows how hard it is to live this way. This tells the excellence of impartiality.

links.reason: Says what it is: each side its due.

couplets.plain: The gains of one who is upright don’t fall apart, and are a strength to those who come after.
couplets.pm: The wealth of an impartial man doesn’t perish as others’ wealth does, and it is a strength even to those of his line. It serves him too as long as he lives. It lasts because it comes with righteousness. Descendants are called what remains after you die.

links.quote: a strength to those who come after
links.reason: Promises the upright gains that last and strengthen those who come after.

couplets.plain: Even if it brings only good, let go at once of gain that comes from leaving the middle.
couplets.pm: Even if it brings nothing but good, give up at once any gain that comes from abandoning impartiality. He says “even if” because such gain brings no good. These two couplets say that wealth from impartiality does good and other wealth does harm.

links.quote: gain that comes from leaving the middle
links.reason: Refuses gain won by leaving the middle, even where it promises nothing but good.

couplets.plain: Whether people are worthy or unworthy is seen by what each leaves behind.
couplets.pm: Whether someone is impartial or not can be known from whether they have good sons. It is certain that the worthy have descendants and the unworthy don’t, so this is the sign for telling the two apart.
couplets.note: எச்சம், what is left after you, could be a name or deeds as well as children. He takes it as good sons.

couplets.plain: Loss and gain will always come. A heart that doesn’t lean is the ornament of the worthy.
couplets.pm: Ruin from bad deeds and increase from good deeds are laid down beforehand for everyone. Knowing this, not to lean in your heart because of them is the beauty of the wise. To lean is to take one side, thinking these come now, to avoid ruin or win increase. Their cause is past deeds, not leaning.

links.reason: Whatever loss or gain comes, the heart that doesn’t lean is what the worthy are known by.

couplets.plain: If your heart leaves the middle and does wrong, know this: “I will be ruined.”
couplets.pm: If your heart leaves impartiality and thinks of doing otherwise, take that thought as the omen that says “I am bound for ruin.” Thinking is the same as doing, so he says “does”.

links.quote: If your heart leaves the middle
links.reason: Reads the first step from the middle as a sign that ruin is close.

couplets.plain: The world does not count it ruin when someone who stays in the middle and in the good falls low.
couplets.pm: The high-minded don’t count as poverty the poverty of one who stood impartial and stayed in righteousness. They take it as wealth. These three couplets say that loss and gain don’t come from leaning, that leaning brings ruin, and that the lowness of one who doesn’t lean isn’t ruin.

links.quote: The world does not count it ruin
links.reason: Says the world does not count the fall of one who stayed in the middle as ruin.

couplets.plain: To be like the balance that rests level and then weighs true, leaning to neither side, is the ornament of the worthy.
couplets.pm: Like a balance that first stands level and then fixes the weight placed on it, to be sound and lean to no side is the beauty of the wise. Their weighing is grasping, in due order, what is heard through question and answer. Not leaning is stating it as it is, hiding nothing, to enemies, strangers and friends alike.

links.reason: Asks the worthy to lean to neither side.

links.quote: the balance that rests level and then weighs true

couplets.plain: Uprightness is speech that does not bend, if you have made sure there is no bend within.
couplets.pm: Impartiality is having no bend in your speech, provided you firmly have no bend in your mind. The speech is the verdict given in due order. Joined to a mind that leans for no reason, saying what righteousness requires is impartial. Without that mind, the same words are not.

links.reason: Grants uprightness to the words of one with no bend within.

couplets.plain: For traders, good trade is to care for others’ goods as their own.
couplets.pm: If traders tend others’ goods as their own, that is good trade for them. That means taking no more and giving no less, weighing evenly. Of these last three couplets, the first two look to those in the assembly and this one to traders, because for both this righteousness matters most.

links.quote: care for others’ goods as their own
links.reason: Calls it good trade to care for others’ goods as one’s own.
